did_you_know.text: The phrase “I may be built up through her” reflects an ancient custom in which a servant’s child could be regarded as the mistress’s child. “On my knees” may express the child’s acceptance into Rachel’s household.
The name Dan is connected with the Hebrew root ד־י־ן, meaning “to judge.” Rachel understands the birth as a judgment in her favor.
The name Naphtali is related to the word for struggles or contests. In this chapter, the names of Jacob’s sons often express their mothers’ feelings at the time of birth.
The name Gad plays on the phrase “fortune has come,” and the word gad is also associated with luck or success. That is why translations render Leah’s words in slightly different ways.
The name Asher is connected with the Hebrew root א־שׁ־ר, associated with happiness and blessing. Leah describes herself as a woman whom others will consider blessed.
The dudaim are traditionally identified with mandrakes, although the plant’s exact identity is uncertain. In the ancient world, mandrakes were associated with love and fertility.

The story of the dudaim gives a small plant from the field great importance in the tension between Rachel and Leah. It shows how people may place their hopes in things whose power has not been proven.
Leah uses the word “wages,” as though the night with Jacob were payment for the dudaim. This economic language highlights the tension and competition within the family.
The name Joseph contains two wordplays: asaf, “remove” or “gather,” and yosef, “may he add.” Rachel celebrates the son she has received while hoping for another.

The word nichashti is related to the Hebrew root נ־ח־שׁ, also connected with the word “snake.” Here Laban says that he has learned, perhaps through observation or signs, that his success is linked to Jacob.

The words “streaked,” “spotted,” and “speckled” describe different coat patterns in the animals. Such precise descriptions were especially important when livestock were being divided or used as payment.

Placing striped sticks by the watering troughs reflects an ancient belief that what animals saw while mating could affect their offspring. Modern genetics does not support this as a cause of changes in coat color.

Jacob does more than use the sticks: he also separates the flocks and manages the breeding differently. The chapter therefore presents a combination of practical planning, observation, and an attempt to gain an advantage.

The list of sheep, servants, camels, and donkeys portrays the wealth of a nomadic family leader. In the ancient world, the size of one’s flocks and herds was a major measure of status and economic power.
